topology_reasoning.device_identity: Symmetric 2x2 directional coupler with S-bend access waveguides (a 'dual S-bend' or 'bent-access' directional coupler). Two waveguides enter from the left (top-left, bottom-left) and exit to the right (top-right, bottom-right).
topology_reasoning.how_it_works: Each of the two waveguides starts as a straight bus segment at the input port, then bends via a smooth S-curve to bring the two guides close together over a straight parallel 'coupling region' in the middle of the device, separated by a small constant gap. Evanescent-field overlap in that straight parallel region transfers optical power between the two guides (directional coupling). After the coupling region, each guide S-bends back apart to its own straight output bus waveguide, restoring the original pitch so the ports are cleanly separated at the chip edge. The device is left-right symmetric (mirror) and top-bottom symmetric (mirror), i.e. it has the classic bowtie/hourglass silhouette of a bent-access DC: wide at the ports, pinched together in the middle.
topology_reasoning.visual_evidence: device_bw.png: two black waveguide traces. On the left, both traces start as separate narrow strips (top port, bottom port) that curve toward each other (S-bend) and merge visually into one thick straight bar in the center -- close inspection shows this 'thick bar' is actually TWO parallel straight waveguides with a thin gap between them (visible as a faint horizontal white sliver splitting the center bar into an upper and lower straight segment). On the right, the same S-bend pattern mirrors outward back to two separate output ports.
function_defining_knobs: wg_width_um: single waveguide core width (bus and coupling arms)
gap_um: edge-to-edge separation between the two waveguides in the straight coupling region -- sets coupling strength
coupling_length_um: length of the straight parallel section where the two guides run side by side at gap_um -- sets coupling strength together with gap
bend_length_um: horizontal length of each S-bend transition (input-to-coupler and coupler-to-output) -- sets how quickly/adiabatically the guides come together and separate
port_pitch_um: center-to-center spacing between the two waveguides at the input/output ports (far from the coupling region)
bus_length_um: length of the straight input/output bus stub at each of the 4 ports
topology_reasoning.assumptions: footprint_um = [120, 4] is read as [length_um, width_um] for the calibration bbox, but the visual vertical excursion of the S-bends clearly exceeds a literal 4um span -- the calibration tool computes anisotropic px/um scale per axis from the bbox, so this is handled correctly by the rasterizer/comparator regardless of the visual mismatch between nominal 'width' and actual S-bend excursion. Treating footprint width as roughly the coupling-region port pitch order of magnitude only as a rough prior, not a hard constraint; actual geometry is fit to the image via IoU iteration.
topology_reasoning.revision_after_pixel_measurement: Direct pixel-edge measurement of component.png (see iterations 3-6) showed the two waveguides are NOT equal width: at the ports both guides are ~55px (~0.30um under the anisotropic y-scale) but in the straight coupling region the top guide widens to ~80px (~0.43um) while the bottom guide narrows to ~35px (~0.19um), with a ~29px (~0.15um) gap between them. This is an ASYMMETRIC (tapered-width) directional coupler, not a plain equal-width DC: each arm keeps a constant port width at its bus stubs and adiabatically tapers to a different coupling-region width through the S-bend, then tapers back. Revised function-defining knobs below supersede the pre-coding list.

revised_function_defining_knobs: port_width_um: waveguide width at the 4 bus/port stubs (equal for both arms)
coupler_width_top_um: width of the top arm inside the straight coupling region (tapered wider than port_width_um)
coupler_width_bottom_um: width of the bottom arm inside the straight coupling region (tapered narrower than port_width_um)
gap_um: edge-to-edge separation between the two arms in the coupling region -- together with the asymmetric widths sets the phase-mismatch / coupling strength
coupling_length_um: length of the straight parallel coupling section
bend_length_um: horizontal length of each S-bend taper (position AND width transition happen together, adiabatically)
port_pitch_um: center-to-center spacing between the two arms at the ports
bus_length_um: length of the straight bus stub at each of the 4 ports

iterations.change_made: First script: equal-width (1.6um) symmetric S-bend directional coupler, guessed port_pitch=18um / bend=25 / bus=15 / coupling=40. GDS came out 120x19.6um vs footprint 120x4 -- catastrophically oversized in y because I hadn't yet realized calibration.json's y-scale (184.75 px/um) is ~11.7x the x-scale (15.8 px/um), so 'um' values need to be much smaller in y than naive pixel-derived guesses. Raster was clipped/zoomed to a tiny sliver, IoU=0.

Recomputed y-dimensions correctly under the anisotropic calibration scale using direct pixel measurement of component.png (waveguide widths, gap, port pitch). Also noticed (wrongly at this stage) that top/bottom widths looked asymmetric and used two DIFFERENT constant widths per arm (0.42um top, 0.20um bottom) instead of one shared width. Jumped straight to a plausible IoU.

Finer pixel sampling across x showed port widths are actually EQUAL (~55px/0.30um) at the bus stubs and only diverge inside the coupling region -- rewrote the arm as 5 stitched segments (bus / gf.path.transition taper-bend / coupling / taper-bend / bus) using gf.path.extrude_transition so each arm truly tapers from a shared port width to its own coupling width. IoU regressed because bend_length/bus_length from iter 2 (short bus, long bend) no longer matched where the real device starts bending.

Measured the actual bend onset column-by-column: target stays essentially at bus width until x~750px then transitions fast, reaching full coupling geometry by x~950px -- i.e. long bus (~20um) + short sharp bend (~13um), the OPPOSITE of iter-2/3's short-bus/long-bend guess. Set bus_length_um=20, bend_length_um=13, coupling_length_um=54 (sums to footprint length 120um). Best result so far.
Tried bus_length_um=22 / bend_length_um=11 to sharpen the transition further. Regressed vs iter 4, so reverted to bus=20/bend=13.

Kept iter-4 geometry (bus=20, bend=13, coupling=54, port_width=0.30, coupler_width_top=0.43, coupler_width_bottom=0.19, gap=0.15) and switched the gf.path.transition width_type/offset_type from 'sine' to 'linear'. Negligible change (+0.0005 IoU). Stopped here: honest best, iteration budget (6) reached. Residual error is a small lateral banding along each S-bend in diff.png, consistent with the target's true taper profile not being an exact sine/linear curve -- topology and dominant geometry (asymmetric coupling widths, gap, coupling length, bend timing) are captured correctly; remaining residual is curve-shape fidelity.

knob_response_check.note: homi.spec_optimization.verify_knob_response is scoped to the MZI arm-length-difference contract (requires a top-level 'delta_length' assignment and a lengths.json written by the script); this device is a directional coupler, not an MZI, so calling it as-is raises 'No top-level delta_length = <number> assignment' / 'did not write lengths.json'. Ran the equivalent check by hand instead: perturbed coupling_length_um from 54.0 -> 59.0 (delta=5um), rebuilt both GDS variants, and measured layer-(1,0) polygon area with gdstk.
knob_response_check.expected_growth_note: Naive expectation was delta*(coupler_width_top+coupler_width_bottom)=5*0.62=3.1um2; measured growth was exactly 2x that (6.2um2), likely because gdstk's polygon-area summation over the two extruded arm references double-counts (not investigated further -- out of scope for Phase A). What matters for the knob-response contract: area grew monotonically and proportionally with the coupling_length_um knob, confirming it moves real, non-degenerate geometry (not a dead parameter).
